items: A massive heatwave swept across the United States in July 2026, straining the country's power grid and water supplies.
An aquatic center with a six-lane pool, waterslides and a lazy river opened in Quincy, Washington in August 2026.
Texas Governor Greg Abbott called for a ban on building data centres in rural areas during a campaign stop.
The House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act with a vote of 417-3 on September 16, 2026.
Data centers have funded public infrastructure projects in Quincy, Washington including schools, hospitals, libraries and sports complexes.
Residents in Texas testified before state lawmakers expressing concerns about data centers being built near their properties.
Rashida Tlaib voted against the Ratepayer Protection Act.
A Texas legislative hearing on data centers drew so many attendees that lawmakers opened two overflow rooms at the Capitol.
Data centers have funded a public infrastructure boom in Quincy, Washington, including a new high school, hospital, and aquatic center.
Towns and cities across the United States have enacted bans on data center construction.
The U.S. House of Representatives passed the Ratepayer Protection Act.
Opposition to data centers spans political and demographic divisions, uniting both Republicans and Democrats.
Data centers account for 4 percent of U.S. power demand as of 2026.
Data centers are projected to account for 9 percent of US electricity demand by 2030.
Data centres account for 4 percent of US power demand, a share expected to rise to 9 percent by 2030.
Approximately 30 data centers account for an estimated 57% of Quincy, Washington's property taxes.
Data centers account for roughly 0.3 to 0.4 percent of total daily United States water withdrawals.
Data centers created around 900 jobs for engineers, pipefitters and electricians in Quincy, Washington.
The number of active local moratoriums on data center construction in the United States increased to 374 as of September 2026.
The number of local moratoriums on data center construction in the United States increased from 92 in June to 374 by September 2026.
A Fox News poll found 70 percent of Americans opposed to building an AI data center in their area.
About 70 percent of Americans oppose the construction of a data center in their local communities.
The US House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a vote of 417 to 3.
The Ratepayer Protection Act would require data center companies, rather than consumers, to pay for power infrastructure upgrades needed for new large data centers.
The Ratepayer Protection Act creates a federal standard for state utility regulators to require tech and data center companies to pay for power upgrades needed to operate new large data centers.
The Ratepayer Protection Act creates a federal standard for state utility regulators to consider when setting rules on large data centers' infrastructure costs.
The Ratepayers Protection Act requires states to consider putting the responsibility on data center companies rather than consumers to pay for power infrastructure upgrades.
Texas county commissioners currently lack legal authority to impose restrictions on data center construction in unincorporated areas.
Residents in unincorporated areas of Texas are not subject to local codes or restrictions governing data center construction.
Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have proposed a nationwide moratorium on new data center construction.
The Ratepayer Protection Act was brought to a House vote under a fast-tracking procedure known as suspension, requiring support from two-thirds of voting lawmakers.
The debate over AI data centers is a grassroots political movement that cuts across traditional party lines and demographic divisions.
Data center expansion has become a major political issue in United States midterm elections.
Data center opposition is primarily driven by concerns about environmental factors including water consumption, electricity use, and pollution.
Data center expansion has become a source of conflict between communities wanting local control and developers seeking rapid construction.
The debate over data centers involves differing perspectives on environmental and economic priorities.
The most common criticisms of data centers regarding water consumption, electricity use, and job displacement are often based on numbers presented without proper contextual analysis.
Data center moratoriums have become a widespread local policy response to community opposition to new projects.
Community concerns about data centers are rooted in environmental and resource consumption worries rather than abstract fears about technology.
The debate over data centers involves disagreement about whether environmental and resource consumption concerns are justified or overstated.
Data centers function as economic engines that revitalize struggling small towns through jobs and tax revenue.
A lack of county regulatory authority over unincorporated areas is a central problem underlying disputes over data center siting in Texas.
The organized resistance to AI data centers is comparable to the historical opposition that emerged against natural-gas infrastructure projects.
The backlash against data centers reflects existential fears that artificial intelligence will eliminate jobs or even humanity itself.
Skepticism about data centers among people on the political right is dismissed by other conservatives as climate doomerism or Luddism.
Common public criticisms of AI data centers regarding water and electricity consumption are often overstated relative to their actual scale.
Dismissing data center skeptics as climate doomsayers or Luddites mischaracterizes the true nature of the public backlash.
Heat waves strain power grids and increase concern about data center energy consumption.
The rapid expansion of AI data centers outpacing electricity and water infrastructure development creates strain on power grids and water supplies.
Revenue from data center property taxes has enabled Quincy, Washington to fund extensive new public infrastructure and services.
Property tax revenues from data centers enable communities to fund new public infrastructure and services.
Secretive deals involving nondisclosure agreements between developers and elected officials have increased public distrust of data center projects.
Community concerns about job displacement from AI technology contribute to local opposition against data center construction.
Concerns about artificial intelligence eliminating jobs and posing existential risks contribute to grassroots opposition to data centers.
Community concerns about data centers stem from existential fears about job loss and loss of control over technology rather than just local environmental impacts.
The lack of county regulatory authority in unincorporated Texas areas has enabled developers to build data centers near residents without local oversight.
Dismissive responses from technology advocates claiming data center skeptics are hypocritical for using technology have failed to persuade opponents to support construction.
Local opposition to data centers has increased the number of community moratoriums on new construction.
The construction of new large data centers causes higher electricity bills for nearby residential ratepayers.
Water usage by nearby data centers threatens local water sources such as springs and wells relied on by residents.
Grassroots opposition to data centers is driven primarily by concerns over electricity costs, water use, and strain on local infrastructure.
Blocking the construction of new AI data centers in the United States benefits China's position in the global AI race.
Opposition to data centers by some progressives is based on beliefs that facilities should fully cover their own infrastructure costs.
Data center electricity consumption in the United States will increase from 4 percent to 9 percent of total power demand by 2030.
Communities that reject data center construction will experience economic decline relative to those that accept them.
No further significant legislative action on AI data center issues will occur in Congress until the post-election lame-duck session.
The political realignment around data center opposition will continue to split constituencies and forge unexpected alliances across party lines.
The number of local data center moratoriums will continue to increase as midterm elections approach.
The continued lack of federal standards and oversight will lead to more local data center moratoriums and restrictions.
The Senate will consider the Ratepayers Protection Act after the House passed it with overwhelming bipartisan support.
The Ratepayers Protection Act will require technology companies rather than consumers to pay for infrastructure upgrades needed for large data centers.
The Ratepayer Protection Act is unlikely to be signed into law before the November 2026 midterm elections.
Data center policy will remain a central issue in American elections if community opposition continues to grow.
Data center construction will remain a major political issue through the November midterm elections.
Opposition to data centers will remain a significant factor shaping the outcome of the November 2026 midterm elections.
Continued opposition to data center construction will harm the United States' competitiveness relative to China.
Silicon Valley and technology industry interests will face sustained political pressure from grassroots movements opposing data center expansion.
Quincy, Washington's Q-Plex sports complex will open next year as part of the town's continuing data centre-funded building boom.
It is unfair for ordinary electricity ratepayers, rather than data center companies, to bear the cost of grid upgrades needed to power new data centers.
Communities have a right to restrict development that threatens local environmental and quality of life conditions.
Opposing data centers on environmental grounds is hypocritical if one uses internet technology.
Concerns about data centers consuming excessive water and electricity are legitimate and deserve serious consideration.
It is dismissive and unfair for tech-right commentators to treat data center skeptics as hypocrites simply because they use the internet or other technology.
Communities that oppose data center construction harm themselves economically and are choosing to be poor.
It is wrong for communities to oppose data centers because doing so will leave them poorer while benefiting China.
It is unfair for residents in unincorporated areas to lack regulatory protection against unwanted data center development.
Data centers have been a positive economic force for small towns such as Quincy, Washington.
The economic benefits of data centers to local communities outweigh concerns about resource consumption.
The pace of data center expansion prioritizes corporate interests over legitimate public health and environmental concerns.
The secretive deals and nondisclosure agreements that often accompany data center development are unfair to the communities affected.
Data center companies, rather than consumers, should pay for the electricity infrastructure upgrades their facilities require.
Congress should impose a nationwide moratorium on new data center construction.
Congress should impose a nationwide moratorium on the construction of new AI data centers.
States should increase county regulatory authority over data center projects in unincorporated areas.
The state of Texas should give county governments greater regulatory authority over data center projects in unincorporated areas.
Data center companies should be required to generate their own power and reuse water.
Local communities should have authority to make their own decisions about whether to permit data center construction.
Communities should welcome data center development to achieve economic growth and job creation.
The U.S. should restrict data center expansion to maintain geopolitical advantage over China in artificial intelligence development.
Public debate over data centers should rely on data placed in proper context rather than on alarming figures presented without scale.
Policymakers should treat the cross-partisan grassroots opposition to data centers as a legitimate political movement rather than dismiss it as fringe complaint.
Texas should ban the construction of data centers in rural areas.

items: The Southeast Delco School District in Delaware County implemented Amira, an AI-powered literacy tool, as a pilot program in the 2024-2025 school year.
Southeast Delco School District approved a one-year contract for the Amira AI literacy tool on August 28, 2025.
The Southeast Delco School District made the AI reading tool Amira a permanent program for the 2025-2026 school year after piloting it in 2024-2025.
Southeast Delco School District uses the AI tool Amira as a reading tutor for first, second and third grade students.
Southeast Delco School District uses the AI literacy tool Amira to help identify students struggling to read.
The Amira reading program used in the Southeast Delco School District screens students for dyslexia.
Jason Gibson, a history professor at Alcorn State University, embedded a hidden instruction in his midterm exam that instructed students to place the word Madagascar in their responses.
A hidden instruction embedded in an exam prompt at Alcorn State University revealed that many students had used AI to complete their assignment without permission.
Brown University economics professor Roberto Serrano discovered that 40 out of 86 students in his Welfare Economics course received perfect or nearly perfect scores on a take-home midterm exam.
Brown University economics professor Roberto Serrano administered a take-home midterm exam to accommodate students affected by a campus shooting.
Students at Brown University used AI to cheat on a take-home midterm exam in economics professor Roberto Serrano's course.
New York City announced a one-year moratorium banning generative AI use for public school students from prekindergarten through eighth grade.
New York City's Department of Education banned the use of ChatGPT from school devices and networks in 2023.
Dayton Public Schools implemented a social-emotional learning chatbot named Jordan in collaboration with SchoolAI.
Dayton Public Schools paid SchoolAI $72,600 for multiple AI tools, including a social-emotional learning chatbot named Jordan.
An AI chatbot named Jordan was used in a Dayton, Ohio alternative school to help students open up emotionally.
The Los Angeles Unified School District moved to restrict student access to generative AI platforms while the district reviews safeguards.
Students in China who adopted generative AI experienced a 20 percent decline in their monthly closed-book exam scores within six months.
Researchers at Stockholm University and the University of Hong Kong conducted a 30-month study tracking approximately 27,000 students aged 12 to 18 in China on the effects of generative AI adoption.
Silicon Valley tech families are increasingly using AI-based homeschooling instead of traditional classroom education.
At Brown University, 40 of 86 students in the economics course received perfect or nearly perfect scores on the midterm exam.
32 of 35 students failed Jason Gibson's history midterm at Alcorn State University after being caught using AI.
New York City's AI ban affects approximately 600,000 public school students, nearly two-thirds of the district's total enrollment.
New York City's AI ban affects nearly six hundred thousand public school students in prekindergarten through eighth grade.
A study of 27,000 students in China found that homework scores rose by 18 percent after adopting generative AI.
Monthly exam scores declined by 20 percent within six months after students in the Chinese study adopted generative AI.
Students in the Stockholm University study experienced a twenty percent decline in monthly exam scores within six months of adopting generative AI.
Students in the Stockholm University study spent thirty minutes less on average per assignment after adopting generative AI, falling from sixty-four to forty-five minutes.
Time spent on homework assignments fell by approximately 30 percent in the Chinese study after AI adoption, from 64 minutes to 45 minutes on average.

Harris School students were reading an average of 59 words per minute at the start of the Amira program.

New York City's policy requires students in preschool through second grade to largely lose access to individual devices in class.
New York City's new policy bans generative AI use by public school students from pre-K through 8th grade for one year.
New York City's policy bans generative AI tools for public school students from early childhood through eighth grade.
Under New York City's new policy, high school students are permitted only restricted, supervised use of generative AI.

New York state has banned students from using personal phones during the school day.

Jason Gibson's classroom policy permits students to use AI on exams if they submit appropriate accommodation requests.

AI use in education represents a fundamental reshaping of how students learn and how teachers relate to students.

items: The United States Department of Energy selected five companies to enter advanced talks about using Cold War-era plutonium as nuclear reactor fuel.
The U.S. Department of Energy selected five companies, including Oklo, to enter advanced negotiations over using its Cold War-era plutonium stockpile as nuclear reactor fuel.
Antares Nuclear's Mark-0 reactor completed a zero-power fueled criticality demonstration at Idaho National Laboratory on June 4, 2026.

Antares Nuclear's Mark-0 reactor achieved criticality at the Idaho National Laboratory on June 4, 2026, becoming the first privately developed non-light-water reactor to do so in the US in more than 40 years.
Antares Nuclear's Mark-0 reactor achieved criticality at Idaho National Laboratory on June 4, 2026.
Valar Atomics achieved criticality on June 18, 2026, producing heat from a reactor core in the Utah desert.
Valar Atomics' nuclear reactor went critical inside a tentlike structure in the Utah desert on June 18, 2026.
A lawsuit challenging decisions in the Palisades Nuclear Power Plant restart effort was dismissed by a judge.
A federal court dismissed a lawsuit seeking to halt the restart of the Palisades Nuclear Power Plant in Michigan because it was filed in the wrong court.
The Port of Long Beach signed a cooperation agreement with the Federal Maritime Administration to help establish safety standards for small modular reactors.
The Port of Long Beach has leased space to Bluecore Energy, which is building and testing a small modular nuclear reactor intended to generate electricity for the port and passing ships.
The United States Department of Energy closed on a $1.9 billion loan to NextEra Energy to support the restart of the Duane Arnold nuclear facility.
The Palisades Nuclear Power Plant became the first shuttered nuclear power plant in the United States to resume service.
Palisades Nuclear Power Plant, which closed in May 2022, is in the process of becoming the first shuttered nuclear power plant in the United States to resume service.
Trump signed executive orders in May 2025 setting goals for rapidly advancing small modular nuclear reactors in the United States.
President Trump signed an executive order setting a July 4, 2026 deadline for reactors to reach criticality.
Google agreed to purchase electricity output from the restarted Duane Arnold nuclear facility to power its cloud and artificial intelligence infrastructure in Iowa.
The Duane Arnold nuclear plant in Iowa, which stopped operating in 2020, is being refurbished with NextEra Energy targeting a restart in 2029.
Negotiations between the U.S. Department of Energy and the five selected companies over access to the surplus plutonium stockpile have not yet been finalized.
Twenty-one utility companies covering 95 commercial reactors were surveyed in the Nuclear Energy Institute's 2026 Future of Nuclear Power survey.
Utilities surveyed by the Nuclear Energy Institute are planning for 33.6 gigawatts of new nuclear generation over the next 15 years.
The Department of Energy estimates that improvements to existing nuclear reactors could collectively add more than 7 GW of nuclear generation over the coming decade.
More than 97 percent of nuclear units surveyed are considering or pursuing approval to operate for at least 80 years.
The United States has approximately 20 metric tonnes of surplus plutonium available from dismantled nuclear warheads.
Twenty metric tonnes of weapons-usable plutonium is enough for approximately 2,000 nuclear bombs.
Plutonium has a half-life of 24,000 years.
One small modular reactor developed by Bluecore Energy could power approximately 15,000 homes.
The United States has nearly 100,000 metric tons of used nuclear fuel stored around the country.
Nine of the ten nuclear reactors whose construction began worldwide in 2025 were located in China.
Plant Vogtle's two newest reactors ended up costing more than $30 billion, compared with an original estimate of about $14 billion.
The Duane Arnold nuclear plant slated for restart has a generating capacity of 615 megawatts.
The Mark-0 reactor is the 53rd reactor built at the Idaho National Laboratory site since 1951.
President Trump's May 2025 executive order set a deadline of July 4, 2026, for at least three new experimental nuclear reactors to reach criticality.
President Trump's May 2025 executive order set a deadline of July 4, 2026, for reactors in the Reactor Pilot Program to reach criticality.

The Department of Energy's Reactor Pilot Program allows companies to bypass the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's traditional licensing process, with oversight placed under the Energy Department instead.
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission decided in July 2025 to allow certain exceptions and license amendments as part of efforts to restart the Palisades Nuclear Power Plant.
A 1976 California law bans the construction of new nuclear power plants in the state.
California placed a ban on new nuclear construction in 1976, which may affect the Port of Long Beach small modular reactor project.
Legal challenges to Nuclear Regulatory Commission orders must be filed with the US Courts of Appeals rather than a district court.
The Department of Energy's Surplus Plutonium Utilization Program would, for the first time, allow private companies to use the federal government's plutonium stockpile.
The current wave of reactor start-ups and criticality announcements represents a rebirth of America's nuclear industry.
The nuclear industry in the United States is experiencing a revival driven by the Trump administration's deregulation and support for small modular reactor development.
The decline of America's nuclear industry over past decades is best understood as a self-inflicted policy failure rather than a technical one.
Small modular reactors represent a new technological approach that differs significantly from traditional large nuclear power plants.
The Trump administration's nuclear policy prioritizes small modular reactors over traditional large nuclear plants.
Small modular reactors are positioned as solutions to power artificial intelligence data centers and military applications.
The plan to let private firms use plutonium as fuel reverses a decades-long US policy of avoiding commercial use of plutonium to prevent weapons proliferation.
The United States government is pursuing a policy of making Cold War-era plutonium available to private nuclear companies as fuel for advanced reactors.
Regulatory streamlining has become central to accelerating nuclear reactor development in the United States.
The Trump administration's Reactor Pilot Program represents a significant deregulation of nuclear reactor development by reducing traditional licensing requirements.
Regulatory delay rather than engineering difficulty has become the central obstacle to building new nuclear plants in the United States.
The nuclear energy industry faces skepticism regarding the economic viability of new reactor projects.
The restart of previously shuttered nuclear power plants is occurring as part of broader efforts to increase nuclear energy capacity in the United States.

The push to restart previously shuttered plants such as Palisades, Three Mile Island, and Duane Arnold represents a distinct phase of reviving retired nuclear infrastructure rather than building entirely new reactors.
There is a disconnect between utilities' large-scale nuclear expansion plans and the lagging performance of nuclear-related stocks.
Growing electricity demand driven by artificial intelligence data centers constitutes the biggest energy crisis in a generation.
The current surge in US nuclear development is best understood as a response to surging electricity demand from artificial intelligence and data centers.
President Trump's May 2025 executive order setting a July 2026 deadline directly caused private nuclear companies to achieve reactor criticality within one year.
President Trump's May 2025 executive order setting a criticality deadline caused Antares Nuclear's Mark-0 reactor to achieve criticality by June 2026.
President Trump's May 2025 executive order setting a July 4, 2026 deadline for reactor criticality directly enabled the rapid development achievements of the Reactor Pilot Program.
Trump's May 2025 executive order setting a July 4, 2026 deadline for reactor criticality motivated rapid development of new reactor designs.
President Trump's May 2025 executive order setting a July 4, 2026 deadline caused companies to accelerate their reactor criticality timelines.
President Trump's May 2025 executive order setting a July 4, 2026 criticality deadline caused Antares Nuclear and Valar Atomics to accelerate their reactor development timelines.
Reduced regulatory oversight through the Department of Energy Reactor Pilot Program enabled companies to achieve reactor criticality in less than one year.
China's sustained investment in nuclear reactor construction contributes to competitive pressure on United States nuclear energy policy.
China's accelerated nuclear reactor construction gives China an energy advantage over the United States in supporting industrial expansion.
Decades of costly regulatory delays, exemplified by Plant Vogtle's cost overruns, have caused US nuclear construction to lag behind countries such as China.
Lengthy regulatory processes and cost overruns at existing nuclear plants like Vogtle have discouraged nuclear development in America.
Regulatory burden and lengthy licensing processes historically caused delays and cost overruns in American nuclear plant construction.
Plant Vogtle's massive cost overruns and delays were caused by the regulatory system rather than by problems inherent to nuclear power itself.
Google's purchase agreement for electricity from restarted nuclear plants helps justify federal loans for reactor restart projects.
Google's demand for reliable electricity to power data centers and AI infrastructure motivated the restart of shuttered nuclear plants.
Google's need for electricity to power its cloud and AI infrastructure contributed to the decision to restart the Duane Arnold nuclear plant.
Growing electricity demand from AI and data centers is driving utilities to restart previously shuttered nuclear plants such as Duane Arnold.
Artificial intelligence infrastructure demand is driving utilities to plan new nuclear generation capacity over the coming years.
A $1.9 billion federal loan from the Department of Energy's Loan Programs Office is lowering financing costs enough to make restarting the Duane Arnold nuclear plant economically viable.
Concerns about plutonium proliferation and weapons security are causing opponents to challenge the government's decision to make surplus plutonium available to private companies.
Allowing commercial use of weapons-grade plutonium could enable nations or terrorists to extract plutonium from reactor fuel to build nuclear weapons.
Allowing private companies to use weapons-grade plutonium as reactor fuel could set a dangerous precedent that increases global nuclear proliferation risks.
Legal challenges based on jurisdictional grounds are preventing environmental groups from blocking nuclear plant restart decisions through district courts.
United States utilities will add approximately 33.6 gigawatts of new nuclear generation capacity over the next fifteen years.
Small modular reactors deployed on barges will power coastal ports and maritime operations within the coming years.
Restarted nuclear plants at Palisades, Three Mile Island, and Duane Arnold will collectively add approximately 2.2 gigawatts of nuclear generation to existing capacity.
Commercial use of weapons-grade plutonium in private reactors will establish a precedent that other nations may follow for their own nuclear programs.
California's 1976 ban on new nuclear construction may prevent or delay deployment of small modular reactors at the Port of Long Beach.
Restarted nuclear plants and reactor uprates will collectively add more than 7 gigawatts of generation capacity over the coming decade.
Electricity demand driven by artificial intelligence and data centers will require a substantial expansion of nuclear energy capacity in the United States.
Most existing nuclear reactors in the United States will continue operating for at least 80 years from their initial construction dates.
The announcements of nuclear energy projects will transition into actual construction and operational capacity in the coming years.
Small modular reactors will become commercially operational and begin generating electricity for civilian and military applications by 2027.
America's nuclear renaissance will struggle to move from announcements to actual construction of new reactors.
The plutonium program will enable production of sufficient fuel for advanced small modular reactors to meet electricity demands from data centers and defense applications.
The Duane Arnold nuclear plant in Iowa will resume operations by 2029.
Antares Nuclear's microreactors will eventually be used to power military installations and space missions once commercialized.
Reactors built under the Reactor Pilot Program will begin producing electricity in 2027.
Antares Nuclear's microreactors will be supplying power to military warfighters by 2028.
Bluecore Energy's floating small modular reactors will eventually supply electricity to the Port of Long Beach and the ships that pass through it.
Bluecore Energy's floating small modular reactors will each be capable of powering 15,000 homes once operational at the Port of Long Beach.
The United States has been right to avoid commercial use of plutonium for five decades to prevent nuclear weapons proliferation.
America's regulatory process for nuclear power has unfairly burdened the industry relative to its actual safety record.
Restarting previously shuttered nuclear plants is a beneficial use of America's energy assets.
It is unfair that China is building nuclear reactors at a faster pace than the United States.
Making weapons-grade plutonium available to private companies raises serious weapons proliferation concerns.
Allowing private companies to use the federal plutonium stockpile would set a dangerous precedent for nuclear weapons proliferation globally.
Achieving rapid nuclear reactor development through streamlined regulatory approval is a positive achievement for American energy independence.
The economic costs of traditional nuclear regulatory processes are excessive and unjustifiable compared to the benefits of streamlined approval.
Small modular reactors are a more appropriate energy solution than widespread solar and wind infrastructure for powering American communities.
Small modular reactors are preferable to large traditional nuclear plants because they avoid excessive complexity and cost.
Nuclear power is a more responsible energy solution than expanding wind and solar infrastructure.
The Vogtle nuclear plant's massive cost overruns and delays should not be held against nuclear power itself.
The decades-long stagnation of nuclear power development in the United States represents a serious self-inflicted policy failure.
Treating the large US stockpile of used nuclear fuel as a waste burden rather than a valuable energy resource is a mistake.
The United States should cancel its plan to provide weapons-usable plutonium to private power companies.
Congress should impose stricter safeguards before allowing private companies to access the government's surplus weapons-grade plutonium stockpile.
The United States should streamline its nuclear regulatory process to enable faster reactor construction.
Nuclear power should be an important part of meeting America's growing electricity demands from artificial intelligence.
The Trump administration should use small modular reactors as a central part of its strategy to meet future electricity demand.
Utility companies should plan to extend the operating lives of existing nuclear reactors to at least 80 years rather than retiring them.
The federal government should continue providing loans to support the restart of previously shut down nuclear power plants.
The United States should develop strategies to use stored spent nuclear fuel as an energy resource.
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission's traditional licensing process should be sidestepped for new small reactor designs to speed up deployment.
California should reconsider its 1976 ban on new nuclear construction to allow small modular reactor projects such as the one planned for the Port of Long Beach.
Legal challenges to Nuclear Regulatory Commission decisions should be filed with the U.S. Courts of Appeals rather than federal district courts.
Courts should allow projects like the Palisades Nuclear Power Plant restart to move forward because it benefits domestic energy production.

items.headline: ‘Driving like teenagers’: Waymo robotaxis have run red lights and nearly hit pedestrians, CNN finds
Waymo recalls thousands of robotaxis after some vehicles entered freeway construction zones
Waymo recalls over 3,800 robotaxis following close calls at freeway construction zones
Atlanta Uber drivers say Waymo robotaxis are cutting into earnings, call for protections
Amazon’s Zoox wins first U.S. approval for paid robotaxis without human controls
Waymo Robotaxi Crash Rate 68% Lower Than Human Drivers, Study Finds
Uber lays off 3,300 employees, ceases operations in Nigeria and Uganda
Uber slashing over 3K jobs as rise of robotaxis dents ride-hailing business
NHTSA Opens Investigation into Elon Musk’s Tesla Cybercab
Is DC Too Wild For Waymo? Motorcade Mishap Raises Concerns

items: An unoccupied Waymo robotaxi was swept away in rushing floodwaters in San Antonio.
Atlanta rideshare drivers held a rally calling for protections against autonomous vehicle competition.
Amazon's Zoox unit received NHTSA approval for limited commercial deployment of steering-wheel-free robotaxis.
Amazon's Zoox began charging passengers for robotaxi rides in Las Vegas.
Amazon's Zoox operated driverless vehicles without steering wheels or pedals carrying test passengers in Las Vegas and San Francisco before receiving commercial approval.
Uber ceased operations in Nigeria and Uganda.
Uber laid off 3,300 employees and ceased operations in Nigeria and Uganda.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an investigation into Tesla's Cybercab hours after the company deployed it on streets in Austin, Texas.
Tesla self-certified the Cybercab as compliant with all Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards despite lacking steering wheel and pedals.
Tesla launched its driverless Cybercab on the streets of Austin, Texas.
A Waymo robotaxi stopped in a Dallas intersection and blocked a presidential motorcade during the Republican National Convention.
Waymo robotaxis in Phoenix failed to recognize ramp-closure signs and drove into six freeway construction zones.
Waymo vehicles drove into active freeway construction zones in Phoenix and the San Francisco Bay Area.
Waymo suspended all freeway operations in Los Angeles and Miami after a robotaxi led police on a high-speed pursuit through an active highway construction zone.
A Waymo robotaxi in San Francisco led police on a high-speed pursuit through an active highway construction zone.
Waymo robotaxis have run red lights and driven into oncoming traffic.
Waymo robotaxis have run red lights and come close to hitting pedestrians who were lawfully crossing the street.
Waymo robotaxis had a rear-end crash rate 91% lower than human drivers.
Uber laid off 3,300 employees, representing 10 percent of its workforce.
Waymo robotaxis had a 4 percent higher crash rate than human drivers in Austin.
NHTSA granted Zoox approval to commercially deploy up to 2,500 vehicles in each of the next two years.
Waymo robotaxis have a crash rate 68% lower than human-operated vehicles.
Nearly 3,900 Waymo robotaxis were recalled due to software defects related to freeway construction zones.
Waymo robotaxis posted a 35% lower crash rate in San Francisco compared to human drivers.
Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards require manual controls such as a steering wheel and pedals in vehicles, including robotaxis.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration granted Zoox an exemption from federal rules requiring human controls in vehicles.
Zoox cannot sell any of its robotaxi vehicles to the public as a condition of its NHTSA approval.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration approved Zoox to deploy up to 2,500 vehicles in each of the next two years.
Zoox received a Part 555 exemption from eight separate Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards in 2025.
The Department of Transportation has proposed dropping the manual-controls requirement for self-driving vehicles, but the change has not yet taken effect.
NHTSA's exemption permits Zoox to charge fees for driverless rides without steering wheels or pedals, subject to state and local approvals.
The pattern of Waymo recalls and incidents represents early warning signs of a systemic safety problem.
Waymo robotaxis are particularly effective at avoiding rear-end collisions compared to human-driven vehicles.
Waymo robotaxis create safety problems that are qualitatively different from those posed by human drivers.
The autonomous vehicle industry is experiencing a transition from testing to commercial deployment.
The robotaxi industry faces challenges adapting to complex urban environments and emergency situations.
Waymo's autonomous vehicles have demonstrated significantly improved crash performance compared to human drivers.
The rollout of robotaxis represents a transition toward an autonomous future in the rideshare industry.
Robotaxi companies are using untested technology on public roads before fully resolving safety issues.
Waymo robotaxis exhibit inconsistent performance across different cities and driving conditions.
Robotaxi companies are developing vehicles with novel designs that challenge existing federal safety regulations.
Rideshare drivers view robotaxis as a threat to their economic viability and employment.
Waymo robotaxis create new safety problems despite having advantages over human drivers in some areas.
Waymo robotaxis have demonstrated inability to handle complex traffic management scenarios in high-security environments.
Waymo robotaxis exhibit erratic driving behavior comparable to inexperienced teenage drivers.
Waymo robotaxis are overall safer than human-driven vehicles despite high-profile incidents of erratic behavior.
Uber's mass layoffs represent a strategic shift toward preparing the company for an autonomous, driverless future.
Zoox's regulatory approval marks a milestone for purpose-built autonomous vehicles distinct from retrofitted conventional cars.
Tesla's deployment of the Cybercab without prior federal approval represents a bypassing of established vehicle safety certification norms.
The Dallas motorcade incident exemplifies broader doubts about whether Waymo's technology is ready to operate safely in high-security environments like Washington, D.C.
The Dallas motorcade incident demonstrates that Waymo's technology is not yet ready for widespread deployment in complex urban environments.
Waymo's recall over freeway construction zone failures constitutes a serious safety defect rather than a minor technical issue.
The deployment of Waymo robotaxis in Atlanta has reduced earnings for human rideshare drivers by 10 to 30 percent.
The presence of Waymo robotaxis is reducing earnings for human rideshare drivers in Atlanta.
The expansion of Waymo robotaxis in rideshare markets has reduced earnings for human rideshare drivers.
The growth of robotaxi services is reducing the earnings of human Uber drivers by taking over short, profitable trips.
A software defect that prioritizes avoiding other freeway hazards over recognizing construction zones causes Waymo vehicles to drive into active freeway construction areas.
Software defects in Waymo's autonomous driving system cause vehicles to enter freeway construction zones.
A software defect caused Waymo vehicles to fail to recognize freeway construction zones and ramp closures.
Waymo's failure to recognize freeway construction zone signs contributed to multiple incidents requiring a software recall.
Growth in robotaxi competition has motivated Uber to reduce its workforce and restructure management to focus on autonomous vehicle development.
The rise of robotaxi competition is contributing to Uber's decision to reduce its workforce.
Competition from robotaxis prompted Uber to reduce its workforce through layoffs and exit certain markets.
Rising competition from robotaxi operators such as Waymo is a contributing cause of Uber's decision to lay off 3,300 employees.
Growing competition from robotaxi services, particularly Waymo, contributed to Uber's decision to lay off thousands of employees.
Organizational complexity built during rapid growth hindered Uber's ability to respond quickly to robotaxi competition.
Uber's adoption of artificial intelligence has contributed to its recent rounds of workforce layoffs.
Tesla's failure to equip the Cybercab with steering wheels and pedals triggered an NHTSA investigation into the vehicle's self-certification compliance.
Tesla's self-certification of the Cybercab as compliant with federal safety standards prompted NHTSA to open an investigation.
A Waymo vehicle's inability to independently interpret a complex hand-gesture instruction from a police officer caused it to stop and block a presidential motorcade in Dallas.
Waymo's requirement to seek remote assistance for complex driving maneuvers caused it to block a presidential motorcade in Dallas.
Flooding events caused Waymo to restrict freeway operations after vehicles entered flooded roadways.
The absence of a human driver in Waymo robotaxis creates new safety problems that would not occur with human-driven vehicles.
Human driver inattention causes higher rates of rear-end collisions compared to Waymo's autonomous driving system.
The lack of a human driver reduces certain crash risks such as drunk driving, distraction, and road rage, lowering Waymo's overall crash rate.
Ongoing improvements to Waymo's self-driving software have caused its safety performance relative to human drivers to increase over time.
Rising vehicle maintenance and fueling costs are making it increasingly difficult for rideshare drivers to remain profitable.
The lack of human oversight in Waymo robotaxis enables rapid deployment without adequate testing of edge cases.
Waymo robotaxis will expand into additional cities beyond the 11 cities where they currently operate.
Waymo will reduce its reliance on remote human assistance to operate its vehicles more autonomously in the future.
Zoox will expand its paid robotaxi service from Las Vegas to additional markets after completing state regulatory requirements.
Regulatory approval processes for autonomous vehicles will continue to extend commercialization timelines for manufacturers.
Federal regulators will continue to scrutinize and potentially limit the deployment of vehicles without steering wheels or pedals until new safety standards are finalized.
NHTSA's investigation into Tesla's Cybercab will delay or restrict the vehicle's path to commercial deployment.
Waymo robotaxis will face administrative or political obstacles to operating in Washington, D.C. due to concerns about handling security-related traffic events.
Waymo will not be permitted to deploy fully driverless vehicles on Washington, D.C. streets due to security concerns.
Washington, D.C. officials will resist approving Waymo's deployment due to concerns about its Chinese-manufactured vehicles and readiness for the city's security demands.
Robotaxi companies will need to address technical limitations before operating safely in high-security urban environments.
Waymo's crash rate relative to human drivers will improve further as its self-driving software continues to be refined.
The growth of autonomous vehicles will continue to reduce the availability of profitable short-distance trips for human rideshare drivers.
Uber's cost-cutting measures will generate savings that the company will reinvest in growth and innovation.
Waymo robotaxis are demonstrably safer than human drivers based on statistical crash data.
It is unfair for autonomous vehicle companies to displace human rideshare drivers without providing economic protections.
The use of Chinese-manufactured autonomous vehicles in sensitive U.S. locations poses an unacceptable national security risk.
Waymo's pattern of dangerous incidents, including running red lights and entering flooded or active construction zones, represents a serious safety failure given the risk to human life.
It is wrong for Waymo to deploy robotaxis in cities before their software can reliably handle complex situations like construction zones and floods.
It is unfair for autonomous vehicle makers to certify their own robotaxis as meeting federal safety standards rather than have an independent body verify compliance before deployment.
It is wrong for Tesla to self-certify the Cybercab as safe without independent verification before deploying it on public roads.
It is wrong to let robotaxis without steering wheels or pedals operate commercially before their safety has been independently proven, as with Tesla's Cybercab and, earlier, Zoox.
Zoox's achievement of regulatory approval for steering-wheel-free robotaxis represents appropriate innovation within safety frameworks.
Uber cutting 3,300 jobs while investing in the autonomous-vehicle future is unfair to the employees who lose their positions.
It is unacceptable for a self-driving vehicle to obstruct a presidential motorcade, regardless of the technical explanation given.
Uber's decision to withdraw from Nigeria and Uganda is unfair to the drivers and riders who depended on the service in those countries.
It would be wrong to allow Washington, D.C.'s streets to serve as a testing ground for autonomous vehicles given the security risks posed to presidential motorcades and other sensitive operations.
Policymakers should implement protections for rideshare drivers whose earnings are being reduced by the growth of robotaxi services.
Federal regulations should be updated to remove requirements for human controls in fully autonomous vehicles before they are deployed commercially.
Federal regulators should keep requiring robotaxis to have human controls such as steering wheels and pedals rather than granting exemptions from that rule.
Companies deploying autonomous vehicles should reduce their reliance on remote human assistance before expanding to new markets.
Companies deploying autonomous vehicles should establish remote assistance capabilities to handle complex traffic situations.
Waymo should not expand its driverless service into Washington, D.C. until it can reliably handle presidential motorcades and sudden street closures.
Washington D.C. should restrict autonomous vehicle testing until they demonstrate capability in high-security environments.
Waymo should restrict its vehicles from freeway driving until software defects related to construction zone recognition are fully resolved.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration should investigate the process Tesla used to self-certify its driverless Cybercab as meeting federal safety standards.
NHTSA should require autonomous vehicle companies like Tesla to provide full technical data justifying self-certification before allowing driverless vehicles on public roads.
Regulatory agencies should conduct formal audits of robotaxi self-certifications before permitting commercial operations.
Companies operating autonomous vehicles should proactively notify regulators and issue recalls as soon as software defects are identified, as Waymo did with its construction-zone and flooding issues.
Governments should impose stricter regulations on autonomous vehicle companies expanding into new cities.
Autonomous vehicle companies should restrict their operations in areas with complex traffic patterns until technology improvements are verified.
Robotaxi operators should restrict operations in areas with unpredictable security events until their systems are adequately tested.
Rideshare platforms like Uber should invest in technologies and strategies that complement human drivers rather than replace them entirely.
Uber should reinvest the savings from its 2026 layoffs into growth, innovation, and autonomous vehicle capabilities.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration should grant exemptions from traditional human-control safety standards to purpose-built autonomous vehicles like Zoox's robotaxi.

items: The US Supreme Court ruled that the Trump administration's use of emergency powers to impose tariffs on dozens of countries was unlawful.
The United States and China agreed to slash tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods under a 30-for-30 framework following a meeting between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Major US retailers and companies including Walmart, Target, and Apple received large tariff refunds following the Supreme Court's ruling.
Most US businesses that received tariff refunds are not passing the savings on to consumers.
President Trump announced a plan to temporarily lower tariff rates on imported ground beef and allow up to 300,000 metric tons to enter with no out-of-quota tariff.
President Trump announced that Mesabi Metallics will build a $15 billion steel plant in Iowa.
Canada lost approximately 41,700 jobs in August 2026, contrary to analyst expectations for a gain of 15,000 jobs.
The Yale Budget Lab estimated that Trump's tariffs cost US households approximately $1,000 per year.
US soybeans were excluded from the list of US agricultural products eligible for reduced Chinese tariffs in the 30-for-30 framework.
US manufacturing orders rose in July 2026.
The Trump administration collected approximately $166 billion in tariff revenues before the Supreme Court struck down the tariff regime.
As of July 31, 2026, the US government had refunded $100 billion of the tariffs it had collected.
As of July 31, 2026, the US government had issued $100 billion in tariff refunds out of $168 billion collected.
The US government collected about $166 billion to $168 billion in tariff revenue from roughly 330,000 importers before the Supreme Court ruling.
Walmart received a tariff refund of $2.9 billion.
The average cost of a pound of ground beef in the United States increased nearly 57 percent over a five-year period.
New factory orders in the United States rose 0.9 percent in July 2026 to $663.6 billion.
Manufacturing orders for industrial machinery and nondefense communications equipment rose approximately 40 percent in the first seven months of 2026.
Primary metals factory orders increased 14.4 percent in the first seven months of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025.
The tariff refunds are estimated to add approximately 0.2 percentage points to third-quarter 2026 GDP growth.
Tariffs cost the average American household about $1,000 a year.
Nearly 200,000 manufacturing jobs were lost in the year before Trump took office in 2025.
The Mesabi Metallics steel plant in Iowa is projected to cost $15 billion.
The US-China tariff reduction agreement covers $60 billion worth of goods.
The US Court of International Trade ruled that companies affected by the invalidated tariffs should be refunded.
Under the new US-China "30-for-30" framework, each country may import $30 billion worth of non-sensitive goods from the other at reduced tariff rates.
The US Supreme Court ruled that President Trump exceeded his authority by invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to impose fentanyl-related and reciprocal tariffs.
The Trump administration's tariffs under the Trade Expansion Act on steel, automobiles and copper were upheld by the Supreme Court.
A Section 232 tariff imposes a 50 percent duty on imported steel.
President Trump's ground beef plan allows up to 300,000 metric tons of imported ground beef to enter the US without an out-of-quota tariff.
The US manufacturing sector is experiencing a significant expansion with rising orders and job openings across multiple industries.
The Trump administration's tariff regime constituted an emergency use of presidential power under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
The tariff refunds represent a financial windfall for major US corporations but not for ordinary consumers.
The situation represents a reversal of the usual political logic about tariff policy, where costs have become highly visible to voters.
The tariff dispute between the United States and Canada has disproportionately affected vulnerable Canadian sectors such as wood products.
Trump's tariff policy is best understood as a broken campaign promise to lower costs for American consumers.
The US Supreme Court's February 2026 ruling represents a major legal defeat for the Trump administration's use of emergency powers to impose tariffs.
The new US-China tariff agreement marks a de-escalation of the long-running trade war between the two countries.
The new US-China tariff deal is an effort to stabilize a relationship that has historically been volatile and contentious.
The new US-China tariff arrangement is a limited reciprocal reduction rather than a comprehensive resolution of the trade dispute.
Trump's tariff program is a centerpiece of his overall trade agenda rather than an isolated policy.
Trump's steel tariffs are the centerpiece of his administration's broader trade agenda to boost domestic manufacturing.
The ongoing tariff dispute between the United States and Canada constitutes a trade war.
Trump's tariff policy has shifted from a political asset that won him the presidency to a potential liability for Republicans in Congress.
Tariffs are best understood as a policy that raises costs for ordinary consumers more than it delivers them benefits.
The current expansion in US manufacturing represents a genuine increase in real physical output rather than just higher prices.
The tariff refunds issued after the Supreme Court ruling amount to a temporary economic stimulus rather than a lasting policy shift.
Tariff refunds contributed to a boost in US third-quarter GDP growth in 2026.
Escalating US-Canada trade tensions caused job losses in Canada's trade-exposed sectors in August 2026.
The visibility of consumer price increases from tariffs has reduced public support for Trump's tariff policy.
Trump's tariff policies contributed to declining support for Republicans among voters concerned about the cost of living.
Trump's 50 percent Section 232 steel tariff contributed to a resurgence in US steel production and investment.
Higher tariff costs have contributed to increased ground beef prices over the past five years.
Tariffs caused many US businesses to raise consumer prices to cover the added costs.
The Supreme Court's ruling against the IEEPA tariffs caused the US government to issue over $100 billion in refunds to importers.
The difficulty of isolating tariff costs from other pricing factors is why businesses are not passing tariff refunds on to consumers.
The inability to determine precisely how much consumers paid in higher prices due to tariffs prevents accurate refund calculations to individual consumers.
Tariff protection and government support for domestic steel production enabled the announcement of a major new steel plant in Iowa.
Trump's trade and manufacturing policies are contributing to the strong growth in US factory orders and industrial production seen in 2026.
Trump's plan to lower tariffs on imported ground beef will not significantly reduce hamburger prices for consumers.
Canada will experience further job losses as the full 50 percent US tariffs take effect.
The US-China tariff reduction agreement will improve market access for American exporters to China.
The tariff reduction agreement between the United States and China will improve market access for approximately 30 percent of US exports to China.
The tariff reduction agreement between the US and China will not significantly benefit American soybean farmers.
Economic growth without tariff refunds would have been weaker than the 4% projected rate in the third quarter.
Trump's tariff policy will hurt Republican electoral prospects in the November 2026 midterm elections.
The new Mesabi Metallics steel plant in Iowa will create approximately 1,750 permanent jobs once operational.
The Mesabi Metallics steel plant in Iowa will create thousands of new jobs once it becomes operational.
The Mesabi Metallics steel plant will add tens of billions of dollars to the US economy.
The Mesabi Metallics steel plant will produce millions of tons of steel annually once fully operational in 2030.
Consumers will receive little or no refund money from businesses that got government tariff refunds.
The tariff refunds and temporary boost to economic growth will prove insufficient to maintain support for Trump's overall tariff policy through the midterm elections.
It is unfair that businesses received tariff refunds while consumers who paid higher prices will see little or no refund money.
Trump's use of emergency powers to impose tariffs without sufficient legal authority was wrong.
The Supreme Court was wrong to rule that Trump exceeded his authority by using emergency powers to impose tariffs.
Tariff policies that increase costs for ordinary households while benefiting specific industries are economically unfair.
The economic and household costs of Trump's tariffs outweigh whatever political or economic benefits they provide to protected industries.
It is good that the United States is rebuilding its domestic steel manufacturing capacity.
The new Mesabi Metallics steel plant in Iowa is a positive outcome of Trump's steel tariff policy.
It is unfair that American soybean farmers were left out of the tariff reductions in the new US-China trade agreement.
Trump's tariff policy has harmed Canadian workers unfairly as collateral damage in a trade dispute.
Reducing tariffs between the U.S. and China on non-sensitive goods is a positive development for both economies.
Trump's tariff policy has been bad for the working-class voters it was intended to help.
It is unfair to U.S. ranchers that Trump's plan to import cheaper foreign beef undercuts domestic beef producers.
Protecting American manufacturing jobs through tariffs is a legitimate policy goal.
The Trump administration should have complied more efficiently with court orders to issue tariff refunds to affected importers.
Businesses that received tariff refunds should pass the savings on to consumers through lower prices.
Trump should not have pursued tariff policies that increased costs for consumers ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
The United States should prioritize broader trade negotiations with China over unilateral tariff increases on specific sectors.
Policy makers should consider the employment impacts on allied nations like Canada before implementing major tariff increases.
The Trump administration should have complied with court orders to issue tariff refunds to affected importers.
The government should not use tariff policy to influence midterm election outcomes in specific states.

items: A massive heatwave swept across the United States in July 2026, straining the country's power grid and water supplies.
An aquatic center with a six-lane pool, waterslides and a lazy river opened in Quincy, Washington in August 2026.
Texas Governor Greg Abbott called for a ban on building data centres in rural areas during a campaign stop.
The House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act with a vote of 417-3 on September 16, 2026.
Data centers have funded public infrastructure projects in Quincy, Washington including schools, hospitals, libraries and sports complexes.
Residents in Texas testified before state lawmakers expressing concerns about data centers being built near their properties.
Rashida Tlaib voted against the Ratepayer Protection Act.
A Texas legislative hearing on data centers drew so many attendees that lawmakers opened two overflow rooms at the Capitol.
Data centers have funded a public infrastructure boom in Quincy, Washington, including a new high school, hospital, and aquatic center.
Towns and cities across the United States have enacted bans on data center construction.
The U.S. House of Representatives passed the Ratepayer Protection Act.
Opposition to data centers spans political and demographic divisions, uniting both Republicans and Democrats.
Data centers account for 4 percent of U.S. power demand as of 2026.
Data centers are projected to account for 9 percent of US electricity demand by 2030.
Data centres account for 4 percent of US power demand, a share expected to rise to 9 percent by 2030.
Approximately 30 data centers account for an estimated 57% of Quincy, Washington's property taxes.
Data centers account for roughly 0.3 to 0.4 percent of total daily United States water withdrawals.
Data centers created around 900 jobs for engineers, pipefitters and electricians in Quincy, Washington.
The number of active local moratoriums on data center construction in the United States increased to 374 as of September 2026.
The number of local moratoriums on data center construction in the United States increased from 92 in June to 374 by September 2026.
A Fox News poll found 70 percent of Americans opposed to building an AI data center in their area.
About 70 percent of Americans oppose the construction of a data center in their local communities.
The US House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a vote of 417 to 3.
The Ratepayer Protection Act would require data center companies, rather than consumers, to pay for power infrastructure upgrades needed for new large data centers.
The Ratepayer Protection Act creates a federal standard for state utility regulators to require tech and data center companies to pay for power upgrades needed to operate new large data centers.
The Ratepayer Protection Act creates a federal standard for state utility regulators to consider when setting rules on large data centers' infrastructure costs.
The Ratepayers Protection Act requires states to consider putting the responsibility on data center companies rather than consumers to pay for power infrastructure upgrades.
Texas county commissioners currently lack legal authority to impose restrictions on data center construction in unincorporated areas.
Residents in unincorporated areas of Texas are not subject to local codes or restrictions governing data center construction.
Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have proposed a nationwide moratorium on new data center construction.
The Ratepayer Protection Act was brought to a House vote under a fast-tracking procedure known as suspension, requiring support from two-thirds of voting lawmakers.
The debate over AI data centers is a grassroots political movement that cuts across traditional party lines and demographic divisions.
Data center expansion has become a major political issue in United States midterm elections.
Data center opposition is primarily driven by concerns about environmental factors including water consumption, electricity use, and pollution.
Data center expansion has become a source of conflict between communities wanting local control and developers seeking rapid construction.
The debate over data centers involves differing perspectives on environmental and economic priorities.
The most common criticisms of data centers regarding water consumption, electricity use, and job displacement are often based on numbers presented without proper contextual analysis.
Data center moratoriums have become a widespread local policy response to community opposition to new projects.

Return JSON of the form {"stances": {"b0": <integer or null>, "b1": <integer or null>, ...}} with every statement id.

Think about how these statements relate to one another in your own view. Pairs you do not list are treated as unrelated. Judge the relation between the statements, not whether you agree with them. The relation is symmetric, so list each pair once.

Return JSON of the form {"edges": [{"a": "b0", "b": "b5", "w": 2}, ...]}.

items: A massive heatwave swept across the United States in July 2026, straining the country's power grid and water supplies.
An aquatic center with a six-lane pool, waterslides and a lazy river opened in Quincy, Washington in August 2026.
Texas Governor Greg Abbott called for a ban on building data centres in rural areas during a campaign stop.
The House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act with a vote of 417-3 on September 16, 2026.
Data centers have funded public infrastructure projects in Quincy, Washington including schools, hospitals, libraries and sports complexes.
Residents in Texas testified before state lawmakers expressing concerns about data centers being built near their properties.
Rashida Tlaib voted against the Ratepayer Protection Act.
A Texas legislative hearing on data centers drew so many attendees that lawmakers opened two overflow rooms at the Capitol.
Data centers have funded a public infrastructure boom in Quincy, Washington, including a new high school, hospital, and aquatic center.
Towns and cities across the United States have enacted bans on data center construction.
The U.S. House of Representatives passed the Ratepayer Protection Act.
Opposition to data centers spans political and demographic divisions, uniting both Republicans and Democrats.
Data centers account for 4 percent of U.S. power demand as of 2026.
Data centers are projected to account for 9 percent of US electricity demand by 2030.
Data centres account for 4 percent of US power demand, a share expected to rise to 9 percent by 2030.
Approximately 30 data centers account for an estimated 57% of Quincy, Washington's property taxes.
Data centers account for roughly 0.3 to 0.4 percent of total daily United States water withdrawals.
Data centers created around 900 jobs for engineers, pipefitters and electricians in Quincy, Washington.
The number of active local moratoriums on data center construction in the United States increased to 374 as of September 2026.
The number of local moratoriums on data center construction in the United States increased from 92 in June to 374 by September 2026.
A Fox News poll found 70 percent of Americans opposed to building an AI data center in their area.
About 70 percent of Americans oppose the construction of a data center in their local communities.
The US House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a vote of 417 to 3.
The Ratepayer Protection Act would require data center companies, rather than consumers, to pay for power infrastructure upgrades needed for new large data centers.
The Ratepayer Protection Act creates a federal standard for state utility regulators to require tech and data center companies to pay for power upgrades needed to operate new large data centers.
The Ratepayer Protection Act creates a federal standard for state utility regulators to consider when setting rules on large data centers' infrastructure costs.
The Ratepayers Protection Act requires states to consider putting the responsibility on data center companies rather than consumers to pay for power infrastructure upgrades.
Texas county commissioners currently lack legal authority to impose restrictions on data center construction in unincorporated areas.
Residents in unincorporated areas of Texas are not subject to local codes or restrictions governing data center construction.
Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have proposed a nationwide moratorium on new data center construction.
The Ratepayer Protection Act was brought to a House vote under a fast-tracking procedure known as suspension, requiring support from two-thirds of voting lawmakers.
The debate over AI data centers is a grassroots political movement that cuts across traditional party lines and demographic divisions.
Data center expansion has become a major political issue in United States midterm elections.
Data center opposition is primarily driven by concerns about environmental factors including water consumption, electricity use, and pollution.
Data center expansion has become a source of conflict between communities wanting local control and developers seeking rapid construction.
The debate over data centers involves differing perspectives on environmental and economic priorities.
The most common criticisms of data centers regarding water consumption, electricity use, and job displacement are often based on numbers presented without proper contextual analysis.
Data center moratoriums have become a widespread local policy response to community opposition to new projects.
Community concerns about data centers are rooted in environmental and resource consumption worries rather than abstract fears about technology.
The debate over data centers involves disagreement about whether environmental and resource consumption concerns are justified or overstated.
Data centers function as economic engines that revitalize struggling small towns through jobs and tax revenue.
A lack of county regulatory authority over unincorporated areas is a central problem underlying disputes over data center siting in Texas.
The organized resistance to AI data centers is comparable to the historical opposition that emerged against natural-gas infrastructure projects.
The backlash against data centers reflects existential fears that artificial intelligence will eliminate jobs or even humanity itself.
Skepticism about data centers among people on the political right is dismissed by other conservatives as climate doomerism or Luddism.
Common public criticisms of AI data centers regarding water and electricity consumption are often overstated relative to their actual scale.
Dismissing data center skeptics as climate doomsayers or Luddites mischaracterizes the true nature of the public backlash.
Heat waves strain power grids and increase concern about data center energy consumption.
The rapid expansion of AI data centers outpacing electricity and water infrastructure development creates strain on power grids and water supplies.
Revenue from data center property taxes has enabled Quincy, Washington to fund extensive new public infrastructure and services.
Property tax revenues from data centers enable communities to fund new public infrastructure and services.
Secretive deals involving nondisclosure agreements between developers and elected officials have increased public distrust of data center projects.
Community concerns about job displacement from AI technology contribute to local opposition against data center construction.
Concerns about artificial intelligence eliminating jobs and posing existential risks contribute to grassroots opposition to data centers.
Community concerns about data centers stem from existential fears about job loss and loss of control over technology rather than just local environmental impacts.
The lack of county regulatory authority in unincorporated Texas areas has enabled developers to build data centers near residents without local oversight.
Dismissive responses from technology advocates claiming data center skeptics are hypocritical for using technology have failed to persuade opponents to support construction.
Local opposition to data centers has increased the number of community moratoriums on new construction.
The construction of new large data centers causes higher electricity bills for nearby residential ratepayers.
Water usage by nearby data centers threatens local water sources such as springs and wells relied on by residents.
Grassroots opposition to data centers is driven primarily by concerns over electricity costs, water use, and strain on local infrastructure.
Blocking the construction of new AI data centers in the United States benefits China's position in the global AI race.
Opposition to data centers by some progressives is based on beliefs that facilities should fully cover their own infrastructure costs.
Data center electricity consumption in the United States will increase from 4 percent to 9 percent of total power demand by 2030.
Communities that reject data center construction will experience economic decline relative to those that accept them.
No further significant legislative action on AI data center issues will occur in Congress until the post-election lame-duck session.
The political realignment around data center opposition will continue to split constituencies and forge unexpected alliances across party lines.
The number of local data center moratoriums will continue to increase as midterm elections approach.
The continued lack of federal standards and oversight will lead to more local data center moratoriums and restrictions.
The Senate will consider the Ratepayers Protection Act after the House passed it with overwhelming bipartisan support.
The Ratepayers Protection Act will require technology companies rather than consumers to pay for infrastructure upgrades needed for large data centers.
The Ratepayer Protection Act is unlikely to be signed into law before the November 2026 midterm elections.
Data center policy will remain a central issue in American elections if community opposition continues to grow.
Data center construction will remain a major political issue through the November midterm elections.
Opposition to data centers will remain a significant factor shaping the outcome of the November 2026 midterm elections.
Continued opposition to data center construction will harm the United States' competitiveness relative to China.
Silicon Valley and technology industry interests will face sustained political pressure from grassroots movements opposing data center expansion.
Quincy, Washington's Q-Plex sports complex will open next year as part of the town's continuing data centre-funded building boom.
It is unfair for ordinary electricity ratepayers, rather than data center companies, to bear the cost of grid upgrades needed to power new data centers.
Communities have a right to restrict development that threatens local environmental and quality of life conditions.
Opposing data centers on environmental grounds is hypocritical if one uses internet technology.
Concerns about data centers consuming excessive water and electricity are legitimate and deserve serious consideration.
It is dismissive and unfair for tech-right commentators to treat data center skeptics as hypocrites simply because they use the internet or other technology.
Communities that oppose data center construction harm themselves economically and are choosing to be poor.
It is wrong for communities to oppose data centers because doing so will leave them poorer while benefiting China.
It is unfair for residents in unincorporated areas to lack regulatory protection against unwanted data center development.
Data centers have been a positive economic force for small towns such as Quincy, Washington.
The economic benefits of data centers to local communities outweigh concerns about resource consumption.
The pace of data center expansion prioritizes corporate interests over legitimate public health and environmental concerns.
The secretive deals and nondisclosure agreements that often accompany data center development are unfair to the communities affected.
Data center companies, rather than consumers, should pay for the electricity infrastructure upgrades their facilities require.
Congress should impose a nationwide moratorium on new data center construction.
Congress should impose a nationwide moratorium on the construction of new AI data centers.
States should increase county regulatory authority over data center projects in unincorporated areas.
The state of Texas should give county governments greater regulatory authority over data center projects in unincorporated areas.
Data center companies should be required to generate their own power and reuse water.
Local communities should have authority to make their own decisions about whether to permit data center construction.
Communities should welcome data center development to achieve economic growth and job creation.
The U.S. should restrict data center expansion to maintain geopolitical advantage over China in artificial intelligence development.
Public debate over data centers should rely on data placed in proper context rather than on alarming figures presented without scale.
Policymakers should treat the cross-partisan grassroots opposition to data centers as a legitimate political movement rather than dismiss it as fringe complaint.
Texas should ban the construction of data centers in rural areas.
